hook.support: First day at a café. Someone yells “86 the salmon!” and “Behind!” Huh? Every job has its own words. Learn them fast and you fit in fast.
hook.core: First shift in a café kitchen. Someone yells “86 the salmon!” Someone else says “Behind!” and squeezes past with a hot tray. Every workplace has its own language: words, short forms and calls that insiders use without thinking. Crack them fast and you’ll fit in fast, and stay safe.
hook.extend: Kitchens, building sites, shops, hospitals and airlines all build their own language. Jargon, acronyms and set phrases make work faster and safer for insiders. They can also confuse or shut out newcomers. Decoding a workplace’s language, and switching to plain words for outsiders, is a real job skill.

why.support: If you know the words, you can do the job. You also stay safe.
why.core: Knowing a workplace’s language means you understand instructions, stay safe and sound like part of the team. Knowing when **not** to use it helps you talk to customers.
why.extend: Every organisation’s language shows how it works. Decoding it quickly helps you settle into new jobs, avoid costly mistakes, and talk clearly with people outside the team.

articles.title: Every job has its own language

body.support:
Every job has its own words. This is called **jargon**.

- In a kitchen, “86 the salmon” means the salmon has run out.
- On a building site, **PPE** means safety gear, like boots and gloves.
- In a shop, “face up” means move stock to the front of the shelf.
.
Why do jobs use jargon? It’s **fast**. It’s **exact**. It can keep people **safe**. “Behind!” tells people you are behind them with something hot.

But jargon can confuse new people.

How to crack a new word:
1. **Look at the context.** What is happening?
2. **Break it down.** What could the letters stand for?
3. **Ask.** “Sorry, what does that mean?” It’s smart to ask.
.
With customers, use **plain language**: simple words anyone gets.
body.core:
Every workplace builds its own language. Some of it is **jargon** (special words), some is **acronyms** (words made from first letters) and some is set calls everyone knows.

- **Kitchen:** “86 the salmon” means it’s sold out. “Mise” (short for *mise en place*) means your prep. “Behind!” means “I’m behind you, don’t step back.”.
- **Building site:** **PPE** means personal protective equipment: hard hats, boots, gloves. A **toolbox talk** is a short safety meeting.
- **Shop:** “Face up” means pull stock to the front of the shelf. **SOH** means stock on hand.
.
Why does this happen? Insider language is **fast** (one word instead of a sentence), **exact** (everyone means the same thing) and often about **safety**. It also shows you belong.

But it can shut new people out, and a misunderstood word can cause mistakes. So when you hear a new word:
1. **Look at the context.** What’s happening around it?
2. **Break it down.** Do the letters or parts give clues?
3. **Ask.** “Sorry, what does that mean?” Good workers ask. Guessing can be dangerous.
.
And switch it off with outsiders. A customer doesn’t want to hear that the salmon is 86’d. Use **plain language**: “Sorry, we’ve sold out of the salmon.”
body.extend:
Every organisation develops its own language: **jargon**, **acronyms**, **abbreviations** and **standard phrases** that insiders use without thinking.

- **Hospitality:** “86” (sold out), “mise” (prep, from the French *mise en place*), “on the pass” (ready to go out), “Behind!” and “Hot!” as safety calls.
- **Construction:** **PPE**, **SWMS** (safe work method statement), toolbox talks, “make safe”.
- **Retail:** “face up”, **SOH** (stock on hand), markdowns, “the floor”.
- **Aviation and emergency services:** strict **standard phrases**, because a misheard word can be fatal.
.
Insider language develops for good reasons: it’s **efficient**, it’s **precise** among people who share it, and it often encodes **safety**. It also signals belonging, which is why newcomers can feel shut out.

Its risk is that it’s only precise for insiders. To an outsider, or under pressure, a word can be **ambiguous**. That’s why high-risk industries define their phrases strictly.

When you meet unfamiliar language: use the **context**, analyse the **word parts or initials**, and **ask** (precision matters more than looking clever). And know your audience: switch to **plain language** for customers, clients and anyone outside the team.

caseStudies.title: The words that mattered most

body.support:
In **1977**, two big jumbo jets were at a small airport on the island of Tenerife. It was very foggy.

One plane started to take off. But the other plane was still on the runway.

The planes crashed. **583 people died**. It was the worst plane crash ever.

The pilot of the first plane thought he was allowed to take off. He wasn’t.

The radio messages were not clear. Some words could mean more than one thing.

After the crash, airlines changed how they talk. Now, pilots and the tower must use **standard words**. The word “take-off” is only used for the real thing.
body.core:
On 27 March **1977**, two Boeing 747 jumbo jets were waiting at Los Rodeos airport on the island of Tenerife. The airport was crowded and covered in thick fog.

The KLM jet started its take-off run without being cleared to go. The Pan Am jet was still on the same runway. The two planes collided. **583 people died**. It is still the deadliest accident in aviation history.

Investigators found the KLM captain believed he had been cleared to take off. The radio talk between the plane and the control tower was confusing. Some phrases weren’t the standard ones, and part of one message was lost when two people spoke at once.

Afterwards, the Spanish investigators recommended that everyone use **standard phrases**, and that the word “take-off” be kept out of other instructions. Today, pilots and controllers around the world use strict, shared phrases, so a word can only mean one thing.
body.extend:
On 27 March **1977**, Los Rodeos airport on Tenerife was crowded and covered in fog. A KLM Boeing 747 began its take-off run without clearance. It hit a Pan Am 747 that was still on the runway. **583 people died**. It is the deadliest accident in aviation history.

Investigators found the KLM captain believed he had been cleared to take off. The radio talk with the control tower used non-standard, **ambiguous** phrases. The KLM crew radioed that they were “at take-off”. Part of the tower’s reply was lost when two radio calls overlapped.

The Spanish investigators recommended strict **standard phrases** in all radio talk, and keeping the word “take-off” out of other instructions. Aviation now uses a tightly controlled shared language, so each phrase can only mean one thing.

Tenerife is the most extreme example of a general truth. Workplace language is only as safe as it is exact. Shorthand that “everyone knows” can fail right when the pressure is highest.

model.text:
**Workplace:** a supermarket

| Word | Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Face up | Pull stock to the front of the shelf | “Face up aisle 4 before close.” |
| SOH | Stock on hand: how many we have | “SOH says 12 but the shelf is empty.” |
| Markdown | A lower, reduced price | “Put markdowns on the bread at 6.” |
| Code red | A spill. Block the area. | “Code red in dairy!” |

**Why they use it:** it’s quick to say over the speaker, and everyone knows exactly what to do. “Code red” sounds calm to customers, but staff know to act fast.

teacher.overview: Students explore how organisations and industries develop their own language (jargon, acronyms, standard phrases), why (speed, precision, safety, belonging) and its risks (excluding newcomers, ambiguity). They decode a kitchen handover, sort phrases by workplace, and build a jargon buster for a workplace they know, then discuss it. The case study is the 1977 Tenerife runway collision, after which aviation tightened its standard phraseology.
prep: Collect a few real workplace texts with jargon (a roster, a site sign, a stock list) if you can.
Invite students with jobs to bring words from their workplaces.
Be ready to handle the Tenerife case sensitively; keep the focus on language, not graphic detail.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 86 = sold out; 2 mise = prep (mise en place); 3 T12 = table 12, docket = order slip, flag = mark the allergy; 4 safety calls (“behind”, “hot”); 5 temps = fridge temperatures for food safety; 6 DM = duty manager.

**Sort:** on the pass — kitchen (ready to go out); PPE — building site; SOH — shop (stock on hand); toolbox talk — building site; Hot! Behind! — kitchen; face up — shop.

**Case study:** the KLM jet began its take-off without clearance in fog and hit the Pan Am jet; 583 died; non-standard, ambiguous radio phrases and an overlapped transmission; investigators recommended standard phraseology and keeping “take-off” out of other clearances.

realityCheck: **Students with jobs are your best resource.** They’ll know more workplace jargon than any worksheet. Let them teach the class.
**Some jargon is crude.** Set the rule early: workplace words only, and nothing offensive.
**The case study involves mass loss of life.** Keep it focused on the language lesson; check in with any student affected by a recent accident.
**Students without jobs** can decode a sport, a game, a club or the school itself (“SAC”, “VM”, “PD day”).
**Works in a real class:** yes, it’s fun and social, and students realise they already know a lot of insider language.
